newsitem.title: JAPAN: IMF, Japan, U.S.,others set to meet on Thai rescue.
newsitem.headline: IMF, Japan, U.S.,others set to meet on Thai rescue.

text.p: If Thai Finance Minister Thanong Bidaya has his way, Bangkok will ink the biggest funding package for a single country in Tokyo next week since the $40 billion made available to Mexico in 1995.

Bidaya will fly to Japan on Sunday to meet with the International Monetary Fund (IMF) and other institutions as well as about 10 potential donors including the United States and host Japan to secure loans to stabilise the ailing Thai economy.

Thailand has said it is seeking $12 billion to $15 billion in international loans. Thai Finance Ministry sources said in Bangkok on Thursday that it was likely to ask for $7 billion from Japan, $4 billion from the IMF, $1 billion from the World Bank and $1 billion from the Asian Development Bank (ADB).
But international monetary sources in Tokyo said Thanong's visit, scheduled to end on Tuesday, may not give him enough time to obtain results which are eagerly awaited by markets.
Despite its volatility, the Thai baht managed to firm throughout the latter part of this week as the market developed high hopes for the multi-billion loan package.
"Since many parties are involved and we only have a short amount of time, we're not sure whether a concrete package will be drawn up at the meeting," said one monetary source.

In addition to Japan and the IMF, officials from the ADB and the World Bank are expected to attend the meeting along with representatives of China, Hong Kong, Singapore and Australia and the United States.
The U.S. delegation is expected to be head by Timothy Geithner, senior deputy assistant secretary of the Treasury for international affairs.
On Thursday, Treasury Secretary Robert Rubin said the United States would support an IMF package for Thailand once a recovery programme was worked out.

Another Japanese financial source said the meeting will mainly be a chance for Thailand and the IMF to explain to potential donor nations what steps Bangkok will take to improve its economy and what is needed to help the country.
But when push comes to shove, Japan, keen to justify its position as Asia's top economy, has said it is ready to play a leading role alongside the IMF in the planned rescue package.

A senior Japanese Finance Ministry official said Tokyo's contribution to the package would be by far the most given by an individual country and would likely amount to a little under half the total amount.
"Given the magnitude of relations between Japan and Thailand, it is natural for Japan to extend the largest amount of financial help to the country," the official said.

Ministry officials said the total amount of the whole financial package would not be far off the $12 billion to $15 billion in loans Thailand is seeking, adding that the bulk of support would come from the IMF and Japan.
"Any participation (by ADB and ASEAN nations) would be limited. What's important is that they're taking part, not the amount. Their contribution would be meagre," said another ministry official.

Japanese officials said Tokyo's contribution would be almost totally in the form of untied loans made through the government-run Export-Import Bank of Japan. Most of the loans would be over a period of about three years, they added.

In addition to the government, private Japanese banks are expected to join in the support, given their heavy loan exposure in Thailand and the hefty direct investment in that country by Japanese firms.
Japanese media have reported that private banks of Japan and other nations will shoulder a total burden of $5.0 billion.

But bankers said they have yet to receive any formal request for assistance and one senior banker said the framework of private banks' loans could be set later this month after Monday's meeting and an IMF board meeting in mid-August.
Banking sources said Sakura Bank and Bank of Tokyo-Mitsubishi are expected to take a leading role, but Japanese banks may also call for help from foreign banks.
Thailand has nearly $90 billion in foreign currency debt, with Japanese banks having nearly a half of it.
